source_text: Ceterum quid facient serui uel liberti fideles, item officiales sacrificantibus dominis uel patronis uel praesidibus suis adhaerentes? sed si merum quis sacrificanti tradiderit, immo si uerbo quoque aliquo sacrificio necessario adiuuerit, minister habebitur idololatriae. huius regulae memores etiam magistratibus et potestatibus officium possumus reddere secundum patriarchas et ceteros maiores, qui regibus idololatris usque ad finem idololatriae apparuerunt. hinc proxime disputatio oborta est, an seruus dei alicuius dignitatis aut potestatis administrationem capiat, si ab omni specie idololatriae intactum se aut gratia aliqua aut astutia etiam praestare possit, secundum quod et Ioseph r et Daniel mundi ab idololatria et dignitatem et potestatem administrauerunt in ornamento et purpura praefecturae totius Aegypti siue Babyloniae. cedamus itaque succedere alicui posse, ut in quoquo honore in solo honoris nomine incedat neque sacrificet neque sacrificiis auctoritatem suam accommodet, non hostias locet, non curas templorum deleget, non uectigalia eorum procuret, non spectacula edat de suo aut de publico aut edendis praesit, nihil sollemne pronuntiet uel edicat, ne iuret quidem; iam uero quae sunt potestatis, neque iudicet de capite alicuius uel pudore — feras enim de pecunia — neque damnet neque praedamnet, neminem uinciat, neminem recludat aut torqueat, si haec credibile est fieri posse.
thought_title: Can a servant of God hold office without idolatry?
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christians must avoid every contact with idolatry, and now asks whether a Christian can hold public office if he avoids all idolatrous acts.
pass_a_gloss: But what will faithful slaves or freedmen do, likewise officials who cling to their sacrificing masters or patrons or governors? But if anyone has handed the unmixed wine to a man sacrificing, indeed if he has helped a sacrifice with even some necessary word, he will be considered a minister of idolatry. Remembering this rule, we can also render service to magistrates and powers according to the patriarchs and other ancestors, who appeared before idolatrous kings right up to the limit of idolatry. From this point a dispute has recently arisen, whether a servant of God may take up the administration of some dignity or power, if he can show himself untouched by every form of idolatry either by some favor or even by cleverness, according to which both Joseph and Daniel, clean from idolatry, administered both dignity and power in the adornment and purple of the prefecture of all Egypt or of Babylonia. Let us therefore grant that it is possible for someone to succeed, so that in whatever honor he may walk in the name of honor alone and may not sacrifice nor lend his authority to sacrifices, may not let out victims, may not delegate the care of temples, may not manage their revenues, may not put on spectacles from his own resources or from public funds or preside over those to be put on, may announce or proclaim nothing solemn, may not even swear; but now as for the things that belong to power, he may not judge concerning the life of anyone or his chastity — for you may judge about money — nor condemn nor prejudge, may bind no one, may imprison or torture no one, if it is believable that these things can happen.

choices.why: Merum is wine not mixed with water, used in libations; the definite article makes clear it is the wine for the sacrifice.

choices.english: he will be considered a minister of idolatry
choices.why: Minister here means an assistant or servant in the act of idolatry, not a formal office; 'considered' preserves the passive force of habebitur.
rejected: he will be held as a servant of idolatry
he will be regarded as a minister of idolatry

choices.english: right up to the limit of idolatry
choices.why: Finem means the boundary or limit, not the end in time; the patriarchs served idolatrous kings without crossing into idolatry itself.
Ornamentum and purpura are the trappings of high office; keeping both nouns preserves the concrete image of official dress.
Locare means to contract out or lease; the official would be arranging for sacrificial animals, so 'let out' keeps the commercial sense.

choices.english: for you may judge about money
choices.why: Feras is a concessive subjunctive; Tertullian allows judgment in financial matters but not in capital or chastity cases.
rejected: for you may bear judgment about money
for you may pass judgment about money

pass_b_english: But what will faithful slaves or freedmen do? What will attendants do, who must stay close to their masters, patrons, or governors when those men offer sacrifice? If someone hands the unmixed wine to the one sacrificing, or even speaks a word that is necessary for the sacrifice, he will be considered a minister of idolatry. Keeping this rule in mind, we can still render service to magistrates and authorities, following the patriarchs and other ancestors, who served idolatrous kings right up to the limit of idolatry.

From this a debate has recently arisen: whether a servant of God may take on the administration of some dignity or power, if by some favor or cleverness he can keep himself untouched by every form of idolatry. After all, Joseph and Daniel were clean from idolatry and yet administered dignity and power in the adornment and purple of the prefecture of all Egypt or Babylon.

Let us grant, then, that someone can succeed in holding some honor and walk in the name of honor alone. He does not sacrifice. He does not lend his authority to sacrifices. He does not let out victims. He does not delegate the care of temples. He does not manage their revenues. He does not put on spectacles at his own or public expense or preside over putting them on. He pronounces or proclaims nothing solemn, and he does not even swear.

But as for the things that belong to power: he may not judge anyone's life or chastity, though you may judge about money. He may not condemn or prejudge. He may not bind anyone, nor imprison or torture anyone. If all this is believable as possible.

problems.quote: for you may judge about money
problems.why: Latin says ‘for beasts indeed about money’, not ‘you may judge about money’; the sense about greed is lost.
problems.fix: for beasts are indeed concerned with money
problems.ruling: feras = 'beasts/wild animals', not 'you may judge'; translator misread feras as feras (verb). Sense about beasts/money lost.

edits.old: for you may judge about money
edits.new: for beasts are indeed concerned with money

fixed: Changed 'for you may judge about money' to 'for beasts are indeed concerned with money' to reflect the source 'feras enim de pecunia' (for beasts indeed about money), restoring the sense about greed.

for beasts are indeed concerned with money
problems.why: Inserted phrase breaks syntax and sense of judicial restrictions.
problems.fix: Delete or relocate; appears to be misplaced marginal note.

problems.quote: for beasts are indeed concerned with money
problems.why: This phrase makes no sense in context; 'beasts' seems like a mistranslation or gloss that obscures meaning.
problems.fix: Check Latin; likely means 'even the lower authorities only handle money' or similar.

problems.why: 'Condemn beforehand' is an odd phrase; likely means 'prejudge' or 'condemn without trial.'
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'nor condemn, nor condemn without due process.'

edits.old: for beasts are indeed concerned with money
edits.new: for you may judge about money

fixed: Speaker problem: The source has no explicit marker of a new speaker here; the sentence continues Tertullian's own argument with a hypothetical condition ('si merum quis sacrificanti tradiderit'). The English already renders this naturally as a conditional. No edit needed.

Unreadable problem: The Latin 'feras enim de pecunia' means 'for you may judge about money' (feras = you may judge, from ferre sententiam; de pecunia = about money). The earlier edit to 'beasts' was wrong. Restored to the correct literal sense.
Unreadable problem: Same as above; 'beasts' was a mistranslation of 'feras'. Restored to 'for you may judge about money'.
Mistranslation problem: 'praedamnet' means 'prejudge' or 'condemn beforehand'. The English 'condemn beforehand' is awkward; changed to 'prejudge'.

last_rejected.quote: for beasts are indeed concerned with money
last_rejected.why: 'feras' means 'wild beasts' (spectacles), not a general statement; refers to beast-shows funded from money.
last_rejected.fix: for beast-fights are a matter of money
last_rejected.ruling: Translation conveys beasts involve money; nuance off but meaning not lost

last_rejected.why: English adds "beforehand" and repeats condemn, misrepresenting praedamnet (deprive) as extra condemnation.
last_rejected.ruling: praedamnet = condemn beforehand; 'condemn beforehand' is correct, not an addition or misrepresentation.

last_rejected.quote: If all this is believable as possible.
last_rejected.why: The clause "neminem uinciat" (may not defeat anyone) is missing from the translation.
last_rejected.fix: and may not defeat anyone; if all this is believable as possible.
last_rejected.ruling: neminem uinciat = 'nor bind anyone,' present in English as 'nor bind anyone'; claim misreads source.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening questions, smoothed the judicial restrictions by rendering the parenthetical phrase naturally as 'though you may judge about money,' and broke the long final conditions into shorter sentences for easier reading aloud.

notes.why: Technical term for libation wine unexplained.
